name: The 'Show as' menu: ways to rescale a dataset
plain: Each layer on the Analysis tab can show a dataset as published or rescaled. Rescaled views include per resident, per square kilometre, share of the island, comparison with Puerto Rico, change since a base year and percentile. The options offered depend on the kind of number.
definition: The 'Show as' list in each layer's Settings. The kind of dataset decides the options. Counts (people, jobs, places, households, work sites): As published, Per 1,000 residents, Per 1,000 housing units (not for jobs, for exposure counts or for housing units themselves), Per km², % of the Puerto Rico total. Exposure counts (residents or housing units inside a hazard, a protected area or near transit) also get % of the area's own residents or housing units, which is how they start. Counts of jobs (25 datasets in the 2026-10 snapshot: total, private-sector and government jobs; tourism-related jobs; accommodation jobs; food service jobs; and the 19 sector jobs) also get % of the municipality's jobs and Location quotient. Dollar totals (total wages, federal awards by type, Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) dollars): As published, $ per resident, $ per km² and % of the Puerto Rico total (not offered for federal loans). All other datasets (rates, dollar levels such as medians and average pay, and ratios): As published, Index (Puerto Rico = 100), Difference from Puerto Rico. Every dataset that is not a one-time snapshot also gets Change since the base year, and every dataset gets Percentile among municipalities.
unit: one of 13 menu options (each dataset offers 4 to 8)

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

method: The functions options, compute and describe of Core.normalize (site/js/core/normalize.js) build the list, do the arithmetic and set the unit and the number of decimals shown. The calculation runs in your browser from the published series each time the map draws. A new shaded count layer starts as 'Per 1,000 residents', a new shaded dollar total starts as '$ per resident', and everything else starts as 'As published', including every symbol layer.
source_detail: Inputs are the Analysis tab datasets: jobs and wages from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW), unemployment from Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS), survey series from the American Community Survey (ACS), population from the Population Estimates, federal awards from USAspending, FEMA dollars from OpenFEMA and tourism places from Overture. The menu is a design choice by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR).
how_to_read: Shade rates and rescaled counts; show raw counts as sized symbols. A shaded map of raw counts mostly shows which municipalities are big. The legend title names the option in use, for example 'Jobs (all employers) · per 1,000 residents'.
caveats: An option changes the question, not the data. A municipality can rank high in jobs per 1,000 residents and low in total jobs.

For share, index, difference and location quotient, 'Puerto Rico' is the island figure published for that dataset. It is not always the sum or the average of the 78 municipalities. Each option's entry says what applies.

'% of the Puerto Rico total' is not offered for federal loans. That series is the estimated cost of loans to the government, which can be near zero or negative in a year, so a share of the island figure would not mean much.

Margins of error are shown only when a layer is shown 'As published'. A value whose margin is wide, or a rate built on very few counted, is marked less reliable in every view (hatching and italics: see measures.less_reliable_values).

values.As published: The dataset's own number in its own unit.
values.Per km²: Count (or dollars) ÷ land area in square kilometres.
values.% of the Puerto Rico total: Value ÷ Puerto Rico value × 100. Not offered for federal loans.
values.% of the municipality's jobs: Jobs in a sector ÷ all jobs in the municipality × 100.
values.Location quotient (Puerto Rico = 1): The sector's share of local jobs ÷ its share of island jobs.
values.$ per km²: Dollar total ÷ land area in square kilometres.
values.Change since the base year: Percent change for counts and dollars; difference for rates and ratios.
values.Percentile among municipalities: Position among the 78 municipalities: 0 is the lowest, 100 the highest.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: add a layer, open Settings, choose 'Show as'

name: Per 1,000 residents
plain: A count divided by the municipality's residents and multiplied by 1,000. It puts a small and a large municipality on the same footing.
definition: Value ÷ resident population × 1,000. The unit is the dataset's unit per 1,000 residents, for example jobs per 1,000 residents or tourism places per 1,000 residents. The option is offered for counts only. The population is the resident population of the same year as the data (a Census count or a July 1 estimate). When the population has no value for that year, the latest earlier year is used, or the first year if none is earlier.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

method: Case per1000 of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: x ÷ popAt(year)[i] × 1000, calculated to three decimals and shown with one. The result is blank when the value or the population is missing or zero. The Puerto Rico row uses the island population. The population is the housing series 'population' (see the entry for resident population).
source_detail: Numerators: any count in the Analysis tab. Denominator: Census Bureau census counts (2010, 2020) and Population Estimates (other years).
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 data show 770 jobs located in San Juan for every 1,000 San Juan residents, against 298 for Puerto Rico as a whole. The jobs are counted where people work, so the figure says how many jobs sit in San Juan, not how many San Juan residents hold one. See 'Workplace basis and residence basis'.
caveats: The population series steps up in 2020 because of a change of estimate base, so a per-1,000 value for 2019 and one for 2020 are not on the same basis.
The denominator counts residents only. Visitors, commuters and people who live in a municipality part of the year are in the numerator (jobs, places, households) but not in the denominator.
For survey series labelled by the last year of a five-year window, the denominator is that one year's population, not an average over the window.

For the five tourism-place datasets the Analysis tab divides by the latest population estimate (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot), while municipalities.json:assets_per_1000_residents divides by the 2020 census count. In the 2026-10 snapshot San Juan shows 10.4 places per 1,000 residents in one and 10.0 in the other.
A small municipality can swing widely when a few units change.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: jobs per 1,000 residents

name: Dollars per resident
plain: A dollar total divided by the municipality's residents. It lets a large and a small municipality be compared on wages, federal awards or disaster aid.
definition: Dollar total ÷ resident population. The unit is dollars per resident, in the dollars of the data year, or in the dollars of the latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) year when 'Inflation-adjusted' is ticked. The option is offered for dollar totals only: total wages paid, federal awards (all types, contracts, grants, direct payments, loans, other), Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Public Assistance obligated and FEMA Individual Assistance approved. Federal awards are obligations (legal commitments to pay) in a federal fiscal year. They are not payments, money spent or a measure of need. Federal loans count at their estimated cost to the government (the subsidy cost), not the amount lent, and can be negative. FEMA dollars are grouped by the year of the disaster declaration, not the year the money was obligated, paid or spent, and Individual Assistance is the amount approved.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

method: Case perCapita of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: x ÷ popAt(year)[i], shown with no decimals and a dollar sign. The Puerto Rico row divides the island total by the island population. A new shaded dollar-total layer starts in this view.
source_detail: Numerators: USAspending awards by place of performance, OpenFEMA Public Assistance and Housing Assistance, Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) total wages, FEMA National Risk Index expected annual loss. Denominator: Census Bureau population series.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, federal awards recorded for San Juan in fiscal year 2025 come to about $42,076 per resident, against $12,068 for Puerto Rico. Part of the gap reflects where awards are recorded: awards to the Commonwealth government for statewide programs are often attributed to the capital (see the caution on statewide awards below). The data do not show how large that part is. The figure is not what each resident received.
caveats: Per resident does not mean that each resident received the amount. Money goes to governments, firms, programs and households.

Federal awards are filed by place of performance as the awarding agency reports it. Awards to the Commonwealth government for statewide programs are often attributed to the capital, so San Juan's figure can include money that serves other places and other municipalities' figures can be low. The data cannot say how much.

A large part of FEMA Public Assistance cannot be placed in a municipality and is recorded as statewide: in the 2026-10 snapshot, 14% of the 2024 total and up to 88% in some years. The Puerto Rico row includes it, so Puerto Rico's per-resident figure can be higher than the sum of its municipalities would give.

The Puerto Rico row for federal awards is USAspending's total for the territory. It also counts awards that name no municipality (21.6% of the fiscal year 2025 total in the 2026-10 snapshot), so it is higher than the sum of the 78 municipalities.
Federal fiscal years run from October to September, and the dollars of a fiscal year are matched to the CPI of the calendar year with the same number.
The population series starts in 2010. In the Trend chart, FEMA Public Assistance values for 2001 to 2009 shown per resident are divided by the 2010 population.

For total wages, the dollars are paid by employers located in the municipality, wherever the workers live. Wages per resident is not residents' income; use American Community Survey income figures for that.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: federal awards per resident

name: Per square kilometre
plain: A count or a dollar total divided by the municipality's land area in square kilometres. It shows how tightly something is packed on the land.
definition: Value ÷ land area in km². The unit is the dataset's unit per km² of land (jobs per km², dollars per km²). The option is offered for counts and for dollar totals. The land area is the Census Bureau's 2020 land area, the same for every year.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

method: Case perkm2 of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: x ÷ land_km2, taken from municipalities.json. Counts are shown with one decimal and dollar totals with none. The Puerto Rico row divides by the sum of the 78 land areas.
source_detail: Denominator: land area (AREALAND) from the Census Bureau's 2020 boundary layer. Numerators: any count or dollar total in the Analysis tab.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 data show about 2,045 jobs per km² of land in San Juan, against 107 for Puerto Rico, whose land area is the sum of the 78 municipalities (8,868.5 km²). A high value marks a dense job centre.
caveats: Land area only, from the 2020 Census. Water is not in the denominator, and the area does not change from year to year.
An average over the whole municipality. Jobs and places cluster in town centres, so a municipality with large rural or protected areas looks sparse even where its centre is dense.
The areas are rounded to 0.1 km² in municipalities.json, which matters little except for very small areas.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: jobs per km²

name: Share of the Puerto Rico total
plain: The municipality's value as a percent of the Puerto Rico value. It shows how much of the island's jobs, dollars or places sit in one municipality.
definition: Value ÷ Puerto Rico value × 100, in percent. The option is offered for counts and for dollar totals, except federal loans (an estimated cost that can be near zero or negative). The Puerto Rico value is the island figure published for that dataset in the same year.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

method: Case sharePR of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: x ÷ a[Puerto Rico] × 100, shown with two decimals. The result is blank when the island value is missing or zero. A shaded count layer is better shown per 1,000 residents when the aim is to compare municipalities of different size.
source_detail: Numerators and island values come from the same Analysis tab dataset.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 data show San Juan with 26.79% of Puerto Rico's jobs and 10.4% of its residents. A share well above the municipality's share of residents marks a place that concentrates the activity.
caveats: The island value is not always the sum of the 78 municipalities, so shares may not add up to 100%. In the 2026-10 snapshot: Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) jobs in 2025, the municipalities add to 943,002 and the island figure is 947,557 (the municipalities hold 99.5%); Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Public Assistance in 2024, the municipalities hold 86% of the island figure and 14% is recorded as statewide; federal awards in fiscal year 2025, the municipalities hold 78.4% and 21.6% names no municipality.
Where a sector figure is withheld for a municipality, that municipality is blank, not zero, and the shares shown do not add up to 100%.
A share says how big a municipality's part is, not how well it is doing.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: share of Puerto Rico's jobs

name: Share of the municipality's jobs
plain: A sector's jobs as a percent of all jobs located in the municipality. It shows how much of a local economy rests on one sector, such as tourism.
definition: Jobs in the dataset ÷ all jobs located in the same municipality × 100, in percent. The denominator is the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) total for all employers (private and government) in the same year, or in the latest earlier year if the data year has none. The option is offered for the jobs family (25 datasets in the 2026-10 snapshot).

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

method: Case shareJobs of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: x ÷ jobsAt(year)[i] × 100, shown with one decimal. Jobs data start in 2014. If you choose an earlier year, the layer shows 2014 (the year shown beside the layer reads 'first data 2014') and divides by the 2014 total.
source_detail: US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages: sector jobs and total jobs.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, tourism-related jobs were 10.0% of San Juan's jobs in 2025 and 10.5% of Puerto Rico's. The Analysis tab's 'Tourism economy' view shades this measure.
caveats: For the 19 sector datasets and the tourism datasets, the numerator counts private-sector jobs while the denominator counts all jobs, government included. Sector shares therefore do not add up to 100%. For 'Jobs (all employers)' the share is 100% wherever it has a value.

Where the Bureau of Labor Statistics withholds a sector in a municipality, the share is blank, not zero. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 34 of the 78 municipalities have no 2024 figure for accommodation and food services, and 39 have none for 2025.
Where arts, entertainment and recreation is withheld, tourism-related jobs count accommodation and food services alone, so the share is slightly low there.

Tourism-related jobs is a grouping of industries (accommodation, food services, arts, entertainment and recreation). It includes jobs that serve residents and does not count every job that serves visitors.
Jobs are counted at the employer's work site, not where workers live.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: tourism-related jobs as a share of local jobs

name: Location quotient
plain: A location quotient compares a sector's share of local jobs with its share of jobs on the whole island. A value of 1 means the same concentration as Puerto Rico; 2 means twice as concentrated.
definition: (Sector jobs in the municipality ÷ all jobs in the municipality) ÷ (sector jobs in Puerto Rico ÷ all jobs in Puerto Rico). It has no unit. The jobs are annual averages from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW), in the same year. The numerator is private-sector jobs in the sector, except for the datasets 'Jobs (all employers)', 'Private-sector jobs' and 'Government jobs', which count what their names say. Both denominators count all jobs, government included. The option is offered for the jobs family (25 datasets in the 2026-10 snapshot).

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

method: Case lq of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: (x ÷ jobs[i]) ÷ (pr ÷ jobs[Puerto Rico]), shown with two decimals. The result is blank when a denominator is missing or zero. Jobs data start in 2014; an earlier chosen year shows 2014. Colours use the diverging scale centred on 1.
source_detail: Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, accommodation jobs in San Juan have a location quotient of 1.26 in 2025: the share of San Juan's jobs in hotels, inns and other places to stay is 26% higher than the island's share. Below 1 the sector is less concentrated than on the island.
caveats: A high quotient means concentration, not size. A municipality with few jobs can have a high quotient from a handful of employers.
Blank where the sector is withheld or the municipality has no such employers; blank is not zero.
Both denominators include government jobs. For the 19 sector datasets and the tourism datasets, the numerators count private-sector jobs only.
For 'Jobs (all employers)' every municipality shows 1.00 (and 100% as a share of jobs), so the option tells nothing there.
Jobs are counted at the work site, not where workers live.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: accommodation jobs, location quotient

name: Index (Puerto Rico = 100)
plain: The municipality's value as a percent of the Puerto Rico value, so that the island equals 100. Above 100 means higher than the island; below 100 means lower.
definition: Value ÷ Puerto Rico value × 100. It has no unit. The option is offered for rates, dollar levels (such as medians and average pay) and ratios. It is a relative comparison: 120 means 20% higher than the island figure, not 20 percentage points higher.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

method: Case index of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: x ÷ a[Puerto Rico] × 100, shown with no decimals. The layer title reads 'index (puerto rico = 100)'. Colours use the diverging scale centred on 100. The Puerto Rico value is the dataset's own island figure (for survey series, the Census Bureau's island estimate), not the average of the 78 municipalities.
source_detail: Any rate, level or ratio dataset in the Analysis tab.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan's poverty rate in the 2020-2024 window (shown as 2024) has an index of 96 (95.8 before rounding): about 4% below the island's rate. To see the gap in percentage points, use 'Difference from Puerto Rico'.
caveats: A relative comparison. A rate that is small on the island can swing the index widely for small changes.
The island figure is not the mean of the municipalities. For medians the island median is not the median of the municipal medians.
No margin of error is calculated for an index. Survey figures for small municipalities can be noisy.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty rate as an index

name: Difference from Puerto Rico
plain: The municipality's value minus the Puerto Rico value, in the same unit. It shows how far above or below the island a place sits.
definition: Value − Puerto Rico value, in the dataset's own unit: dollars for dollar levels, percentage points for percent rates, the dataset's unit otherwise. The option is offered for rates, dollar levels and ratios.
unit: same unit as the dataset (percentage points for percent rates)

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

method: Case diff of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: x − a[Puerto Rico]. A percent rate is labelled 'pts'. Dollars are shown with no decimals, and negative values carry a minus sign. Colours use the diverging scale centred on 0.
source_detail: Any rate, level or ratio dataset in the Analysis tab.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan's median household income in the 2020-2024 window is $1,695 above Puerto Rico's: $27,992 against $26,297.
caveats: No margin of error is calculated for a difference. For survey series, check the margins of both numbers before reading a small difference.
The island figure is the dataset's own island value, not the average of the municipalities.
A difference in percentage points is not a percent difference. Use the index for the relative gap.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: median household income, difference from Puerto Rico

name: Change since the base year
plain: How much a value has changed between a base year you choose and the year on the map. Counts and dollars show percent change. Rates show the change in percentage points.
definition: For counts, dollar totals and dollar levels: (value now − value at the base) ÷ value at the base × 100, in percent. For rates and ratios: value now − value at the base, in the dataset's own unit (percentage points for percent rates, years for median age, index points for the Gini index). On the Analysis tab the base value is the dataset's latest value at or before the chosen base year; the Housing page needs a value in the base year itself. If the year on the map is not later than that base data year, or there is no base value, the municipality is blank. A base value of zero gives a blank for percent change.
unit: percent (counts and dollars) or points (rates and ratios)

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

method: Case change of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js. The default base year is 2014 on the Analysis tab and 2012 on the Housing page. 'Change measured from' lists every year from 2010 to the year before the latest one (on the Analysis tab, the latest year on the year bar; on the Housing page, the latest survey window), so any of them can be chosen. With 'Inflation-adjusted' ticked, both ends are first restated to the same Consumer Price Index (CPI) dollars. The legend title shows the span, for example '(2014 → 2024)'. Colours use the diverging scale centred on 0.
source_detail: Any dataset with more than one year in the Analysis tab, or a Housing page series.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico's poverty rate fell 4.72 percentage points between the 2010-2014 window (2014) and the 2020-2024 window (2024); San Juan's fell 2.10 points. In the same snapshot, median gross rent for Puerto Rico rose 25.1% in nominal dollars over the same span. The 'Change measured from' list ends in 2024 on the Analysis tab and in 2023 on the Housing page.
caveats: Survey windows that share years overlap. Windows labelled 2022 and 2024 share three survey years, so their difference understates real change. The Census Bureau advises comparing windows that do not overlap.
A base year before 2020 and a year after it cross the population estimate break, which can move per-1,000 values and population change.
Percent change from a small base is large. The Ask the observatory chat leaves out municipalities whose starting value is below a minimum for this reason.
Percent change is not meaningful when the base is near zero or negative, as it can be for federal loans (an estimated cost).
No margin of error is calculated for a change. Both ends are estimates.
Dollar changes are in the dollars of each year unless 'Inflation-adjusted' is ticked. The Housing page's change fields are never adjusted for inflation.
Median age is a 'rate' in the Analysis tab, so its change is labelled 'pts' although it is in years.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty rate, change since 2014
Housing page: change maps with a base year

name: Percentile among municipalities
plain: The municipality's position in the list of the 78 municipalities, from 0 (lowest value) to 100 (highest value). It says how a place compares with the others, not by how much.
definition: Position of the value in the sorted list of municipal values, as a percent of the way from the lowest (0) to the highest (100): (number of lower values) ÷ (number of municipalities with a value − 1) × 100. With 78 municipalities each step is 1.3 points. Municipalities with the same value share the lower percentile. The Puerto Rico row is blank. Municipalities without a value are left out and the list gets shorter.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

method: Case pctile of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: the index of the value in the ascending sorted list (first match for ties) ÷ max(1, n − 1) × 100, shown with no decimals. It uses the layer's own settings for year, inflation adjustment and base year.
source_detail: Any dataset in the Analysis tab.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, Guaynabo has the lowest poverty rate of the 78 municipalities in the 2020-2024 window (percentile 0) and Guánica the highest (percentile 100). A percentile of 50 is the middle of the list.
caveats: A percentile ignores distances. Two municipalities one percentile apart can be far apart in value, or almost equal.
Each municipality counts once, whatever its population. It is not a percentile of people.
Municipalities with a blank value (for example withheld sectors) are left out, so the steps are larger than 1.3 points when fewer than 78 have a value.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty rate as a percentile

name: Rank (1 = highest)
plain: A municipality's position when the 78 municipalities are sorted from the highest value to the lowest. Rank 1 is the highest value, not the best result.
definition: 1 + the number of municipalities with a higher value, among the municipalities that have a value. It is written '#19 of 78'. The Puerto Rico row has no rank. On the Analysis tab and the Housing page, municipalities with the same value share the better rank: if three tie for fifth, all show #5 and the next shows #8. The 2D map's Municipality tab note and Rankings tab work differently (see the cautions).

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

method: Function ecRank in site/js/economy.js (Analysis tab inspector and popup) and rankOf in site/js/housing.js (Housing page). Both count the municipalities with a higher value. The rank follows the layer's settings: year, rescaling, inflation adjustment and base year. The Ask the observatory chat's municipality profile also lists a position for each indicator, under the note 'Rank 1 = the highest value among the 78 municipalities'.
source_detail: Any dataset in the Analysis tab, the Housing page series and the tourism place counts.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, Ponce has rank #19 of 78 for poverty rate in the 2020-2024 window: 18 municipalities have a higher rate. For poverty, rank 1 is the highest rate; for income, rank 1 is the highest income.
caveats: Rank 1 is the highest value. Whether that is good or bad depends on the dataset.

On the 2D map, the Municipality tab note ('Rank #n of 78 by tourism places') and the Rankings tab give the position in the sorted list, so tied municipalities get consecutive ranks, not one shared rank. The Ask the observatory chat's municipality profile does the same.
The 'of n' shrinks when some municipalities have no value, so ranks from different datasets are out of different totals.
Ranks use the unrounded values. Two municipalities that show the same rounded number can have different ranks.
A rank hides the size of the gap between neighbours. Use the value, and its margin of error for survey series.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: click a municipality to see its rank

name: Median of the 78 municipalities (Housing page)
plain: The Housing page shows the middle value of the 78 municipalities, the lowest, the highest and the Puerto Rico figure above each chart. The middle value is not the island figure.
definition: The median of the municipal values that have a value in the year on screen: sort them and take the middle one, or the average of the two middle ones when the count is even. Each municipality counts once, whatever its population. Lowest and highest are the smallest and largest of the same values. The Puerto Rico figure is the dataset's own island value, not a calculation from the municipalities.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the year bar or the base year changes

method: Function updateViz and the median helper in site/js/housing.js. They run on the values of the 78 municipalities in the year the dataset resolves to (see the nearest-year rule). The line above each chart reads 'Median of the 78 municipalities, lowest, highest, Puerto Rico'. The words 'the 78 municipalities' are fixed text, so the label still says 78 when fewer municipalities have a value.
source_detail: Housing page series: American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates, Population Estimates and census counts, and OpenFEMA housing assistance.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, for median household income in the 2020-2024 window, the middle of the 78 municipal values is $24,070, the lowest is $16,314 (Las Marías), the highest is $46,731 (Guaynabo) and Puerto Rico as a whole is $26,297. The middle municipal value ($24,070) is not the island median ($26,297). The island figure covers all households. The middle value counts each municipality once.
caveats: Each municipality counts once, so the middle value is not weighted by population and is not the island median.
The label always says 78, even when fewer municipalities have a value in the year shown. Check the ranked chart for the count.
For survey series the middle value uses the estimates alone. Margins of error are not used.

view.label: Housing page: the line above each chart

name: Inflation adjustment (US CPI-U)
plain: Ticking 'Inflation-adjusted' restates dollars of different years in the dollars of the latest year, using the US Consumer Price Index. It lets you compare money across years. The observatory does not use a Puerto Rico price index, so the result is an approximation.
definition: Adjusted value = value × (CPI of the reference year ÷ CPI of the data year). The CPI is the Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U), US city average, all items, not seasonally adjusted (series CUUR0000SA0), annual average, 1982-84 = 100. The reference year is the latest year in the CPI table. The table runs from 2000 to the latest full calendar year at the time of the build, so it holds a factor for every year of every dollar dataset (the earliest is 2001, for FEMA Public Assistance). A year outside the table would take the nearest end of the table. The option appears on datasets whose unit is dollars (dollar levels and dollar totals) and does not change counts or percentages.
unit: dollars of the latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) year

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws; the CPI table is rebuilt with each snapshot

method: Function cpiFactor in site/js/economy.js, applied in ecCalc before any rescaling, so per-resident and per-km² dollars are also in reference-year dollars. In a change layer the base value is restated with its own year's factor. Margins of error are multiplied by the same factor. The CPI values are stored in economy_series.json (deflator.cpi) and come from economy_series.py, which reads the annual averages from the public Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data API (Application Programming Interface).
source_detail: Bureau of Labor Statistics CPI-U US city average, series CUUR0000SA0. Dollar datasets: ACS medians and incomes, QCEW wages and pay, USAspending awards, OpenFEMA dollars, FEMA National Risk Index expected annual loss.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot the reference year is 2025, and $1,000 in 2014 equals $1,360 in 2025 dollars (CPI 321.943 ÷ 236.736). Puerto Rico's median gross rent rose 25.1% between the 2010-2014 and 2020-2024 windows in nominal dollars but fell 5.6% in 2025 dollars.
caveats: The observatory uses the US city average and no Puerto Rico price index. Prices in Puerto Rico can move differently from the US average, so adjusted values are an approximation.

The CPI table starts in 2000, so every year of every dollar dataset has its own factor, including the years 2001 to 2009 of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) series that the Trend chart shows.

American Community Survey (ACS) dollar figures are labelled by the last year of a five-year window, and the factor uses that last year. The Census Bureau's documentation of the 2013-2017 Puerto Rico Community Survey 5-year estimates says monetary values are adjusted to the dollars of the final year of the period with the national CPI. The observatory applies no adjustment of its own to ACS dollars, so they are the figures the Bureau published. The Analysis tab describes them as dollars of each window's last year, and the Housing page describes them as 'not adjusted for inflation' (the observatory itself adds no adjustment). Check the Bureau's documentation for the window you cite.
Federal fiscal-year awards (October to September) use the CPI of the calendar year with the same number. Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) wages are for the calendar year.
The adjustment is one national index applied to every municipality and every kind of spending.

name: Class breaks: quantiles, equal intervals and natural breaks
plain: A shaded map sorts the municipalities into five colour classes. The Analysis tab sets the class limits one of four ways: the same number of municipalities in each class (quantiles), classes of equal width (equal intervals), limits at gaps in the data (natural breaks), or four limits that the user types.
definition: Class limits for a shaded layer whose values have no natural centre. The values of the 78 municipalities are pooled (all years together when 'Same classes in every year' is on) and sorted. Quantiles: the limits are the values one fifth, two fifths, three fifths and four fifths of the way along the sorted list, so each class holds about the same number of values. Equal intervals: the range from the lowest to the highest value is cut into five equal widths. Natural breaks (Jenks): the limits are chosen so that values inside a class are as alike as possible and classes are as different as possible. A value equal to a limit goes in the lower class. My own limits: four numbers in rising order typed in the layer's Settings, which start from the classes the layer has at that moment; text that is not four rising numbers is ignored (the classes stay quantiles until it is fixed). Typed limits apply to a layer shaded alone: two shaded layers together use three classes each, and a scale around a centre (index, difference, change, location quotient) keeps its own cut-offs. A municipality with no value is grey and listed as 'No data'.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

method: The functions make, classOf, jenks and parseBreaks of Core.classify (site/js/core/classify.js), with pool and breaks of the layer engine (site/js/core/engine.js). Quantile limits take pool[floor(n × i ÷ 5)] for i = 1 to 4. Natural breaks use the Fisher-Jenks dynamic programme; when the pool has more than 1,500 values the code runs it on every nth value to keep the page fast. The Puerto Rico row is not in the pool. Bivariate maps use three classes instead of five (see the bivariate entry). The Map layers tab's municipality shading uses quintiles only (see the quintile entry).
source_detail: Any shaded dataset in the Analysis tab. The class methods are a display choice by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR).
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the same poverty data give three different sets of limits (percent, all years pooled): quantiles 41.3, 46.4, 50.5 and 54.9; equal intervals 30.1, 39.3, 48.6 and 57.8; natural breaks 33.5, 41.3, 48.2 and 55.0. All three describe the same data. The legend lists each range and how many municipalities fall in it.
caveats: A colour class is not a verdict. Dark does not mean good or bad, only higher than the limit.
With quantiles, two municipalities with almost the same value can sit in different classes, and with equal intervals a class can have no municipality.

With 'Same classes in every year' on, the five classes are not equal-sized in any single year. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2024 poverty map has 28, 21, 15, 9 and 5 municipalities in its five classes.
Values for years that are not on screen shape the limits when classes are fixed across years.
Typed limits are kept in the shareable link, so a link that holds them opens the same classes.

values.Quantiles (equal counts): Each class holds about the same number of municipalities. This is the default.
values.Equal intervals: Each class covers the same width of values. A class can be empty if a few values are extreme.
values.Natural breaks: Limits are chosen so that values inside a class are as alike as possible, which tends to put limits where the data have gaps. The limits are not round numbers.
values.My own limits: Four limits typed by the user, in rising order. Use them to hold the classes to round numbers or to a policy threshold.

name: Same classes in every year
plain: By default the colour limits are set from all years of a dataset together, so a colour means the same range in every year. When you move the year slider you see real change, not a map that re-sorts itself.
definition: The checkbox 'Same classes in every year' in a layer's Settings. On (the default): class limits, the diverging scale's span and the size of the largest symbol are calculated from the values of all municipalities in every year the dataset has, with the layer's own settings (rescaling, inflation adjustment, base year). Off: they are calculated from the year on screen only, so every year uses all five colours but colours are not comparable between years. The box is not shown for one-time snapshot datasets, which have a single year.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

method: Function ecPool in site/js/economy.js builds the pool: every year of the dataset when the layer is fixed, otherwise the current year only. The limits are cached by dataset, rescaling, inflation setting, base year, class method and year. The Housing page always pools every year and states it in its legend note.
source_detail: Any shaded or symbol dataset with more than one year.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the poverty rate has 78 municipalities × 15 windows = 1,170 values, and they set the limits. With the box on, a map for 2014 and a map for 2024 use the same limits, so a change of colour between the two maps reflects a change in the data. With the box off, the inner limits for 2024 alone would be 37.2, 42.2, 46.1 and 50.3, against 41.3, 46.4, 50.5 and 54.9 when pooled.
caveats: A rate that moves across the whole period can leave most municipalities in the lowest or highest classes in the first or last years.
The legend counts show how many municipalities fall in each class in the year on screen. They are not equal.
The setting is saved in a shared link as the 'fixed' flag of each layer.
The pool holds every year the dataset has, including years before 2010 that the year bar does not offer (federal awards from 2008 and the FEMA series from 2001).

name: Diverging scale (index, difference, location quotient and change)
plain: When a value has a natural centre, the map shades distance from that centre instead of equal-count classes. Red means below the centre, blue means above, and pale grey means near it.
definition: Used for 'Index' (centre 100), 'Difference from Puerto Rico' (centre 0), 'Location quotient' (centre 1) and 'Change since the base year' (centre 0). The span is the largest distance from the centre among all values in the pool. Five classes follow from t = (value − centre) ÷ span: t below −0.5 (strongly below), −0.5 up to −0.1 (below), −0.1 to +0.1 (near the centre), +0.1 up to +0.5 (above), above +0.5 (strongly above). The classes are not equal-count and not chosen by the quantile, equal-interval or natural-breaks setting.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

method: Function ecBreaks (branch for a diverging output with five classes) and ecClass in site/js/economy.js. The colours run dark red, light red, pale grey, light blue, dark blue. In a bivariate map a diverging layer is cut into three classes by the layer's class method instead. The Housing page uses the same rule around 0 for its change maps.
source_detail: Rescaled Analysis tab layers (index, difference, location quotient, change).
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, for poverty as an index (Puerto Rico = 100) the largest distance from 100 among the pooled values is 57.2, so the limits sit at 71.4, 94.3, 105.7 and 128.6. A municipality at 100 is the same as the island; one at 130 is in the highest class.
caveats: One extreme value stretches the span and pushes most municipalities into the pale middle class.
Red and blue show direction from the centre, not good and bad.
The legend lists only classes that hold at least one municipality.

name: Bivariate map (two datasets in one)
plain: When two shaded layers are visible, the map colours each municipality by both at once: three classes for each dataset, nine colours in all. It shows where two things are high together, low together, or differ.
definition: The first shaded layer runs left to right (→) and the second runs upward (↑). Each is cut into three classes (low, middle, high), and a municipality's colour is the pair of its two classes. Each layer's three classes follow its own class method. With quantiles (the default) the cut-offs are terciles. The legend title says 'terciles of each' only when both layers use quantile classes; if either layer uses equal intervals or natural breaks, it says 'three classes of each'. With the default 'Same classes in every year', the terciles are thirds of all municipality values from every year pooled, not thirds of the 78 municipalities in the year shown, so one year can have far more places in one class. Untick 'Same classes in every year' on a layer to cut the year on screen into thirds. A municipality with no value in either layer is grey. A map can shade at most two datasets; further datasets must be shown as symbols.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

method: Function ecRenderMap in site/js/economy.js calls ecBreaks with three classes for each layer and picks a colour from a 3 × 3 palette. Each layer keeps its own year, rescaling and 'Same classes in every year' setting. The legend title names the kind of classes and the legend gives the cut-offs of each axis.
source_detail: Any two shaded datasets in the Analysis tab.
how_to_read: Shade poverty first and median household income second. Each municipality's colour then shows its poverty class along the horizontal axis (→) and its income class along the vertical axis (↑). Read the two axes of the legend, and their cut-offs, before the colours. In the 2026-10 snapshot, with all years pooled, the poverty axis reads 'up to 45.0%' for low and 'above 51.8%' for high.
caveats: 'High' and 'low' are relative, not absolute. With the default settings they compare a municipality with the values of all years pooled, not only with the other municipalities in the year shown. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2024 poverty classes (low, middle, high) hold 44, 21 and 13 municipalities. Median household income, in the dollars of each year, holds 1, 13 and 64.

The legend title says 'terciles of each' only when both layers use quantile classes. Otherwise it says 'three classes of each', and each layer's classes follow its own method (equal intervals or natural breaks). With the default settings, terciles are terciles of all years pooled (see the definition), not thirds of the year on screen.
The two layers can be for different years. Check the year shown beside each layer in the legend.
A bivariate map shows two patterns together. It does not show that one causes the other.

name: Sized symbols (proportional circles)
plain: A sized-symbol layer draws one circle per municipality whose area is proportional to the value. Counts, such as jobs, are better shown this way than as shaded colour.
definition: A circle is drawn at the area-weighted centre of each municipality's largest polygon, so islands and detached parts do not pull it into the sea. The radius is 30 px × √(|value| ÷ largest |value|) (20 px on a phone), with a minimum of 2.5 px. Because area grows with the square of the radius, the circle's area is proportional to the value. The largest |value| comes from all years when classes are fixed. Circles are drawn from the largest to the smallest so small ones stay visible. When the layer has negative values, as change layers do, blue circles mark increases and red circles mark decreases, and size follows the absolute value.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

method: Function ecRenderMap (symbols) and ecCentroid in site/js/economy.js. The legend shows three circles: the largest value, half of it and a tenth of it.
source_detail: Any dataset in the Analysis tab; circles are drawn with Leaflet.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan's jobs in 2025 (253,816) draw a circle of 29.9 px against 30 px for the largest value in any year (255,426). A municipality with 50,000 jobs would draw 13.3 px.
caveats: Below the minimum size the circle is larger than proportional. A value under about 0.7% of the largest is drawn at 2.5 px (about 1,800 jobs when the largest value is 255,426, as in the 2026-10 snapshot).
The eye reads area poorly. Check the numbers in the inspector.
Circles sit at the centre of the municipality's largest polygon, not at the places where the activity happens, and large circles overlap in the San Juan area.
Symbols can be added for any dataset, but they suit counts and dollar totals. The page advises shading rates.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: jobs as sized symbols

name: Nearest-year rule (latest value at or before the chosen year)
plain: One year control sets every layer. A layer that has no value for that year shows its latest earlier year, and a small note beside the layer (the year chip) says which year it used.
definition: For the year chosen on the year bar, each layer shows its own data year: the latest year in its series that is not later than the chosen year. If every year in the series is later, it shows its first year and the year chip says 'first data'. A one-time snapshot layer always shows its snapshot year. With 'Latest' chosen, each layer shows its own last year. The same rule picks the denominators for per-1,000, per-resident, share-of-jobs and location-quotient views.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

method: The function resolve of Core.time (site/js/core/time.js), used by the layer engine (the Analysis tab) and by the Housing page. The year chip comes from E.chip: '2019 (latest at or before 2020)', 'first data 2014', 'snapshot 2026' or, for a survey window, '2016–2020'. The year bar lists the years from 2010 on. Population, jobs and housing units for rescaling come from E.pop, E.jobs and E.hu, which apply the same rule.
source_detail: Every dataset in the Analysis tab.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot: choose 2020, and unemployment from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) shows 2019, because the observatory's unemployment series has no 2020 value, while poverty shows the survey window that ends in 2020. Choose 2012, and jobs show 2014 as 'first data 2014', because the jobs series starts in 2014. Choose 2015, and Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Public Assistance shows 2011, the latest declaration year in the data before 2015. Choose 2025, and survey series show the 2020-2024 window.
caveats: A layer can be older than the year you chose. Read the year chip beside each layer in the legend.

FEMA series have values only for years with a disaster declaration. A year with none shows the last earlier declaration year, not zero, and the dollars are those of that earlier disaster. In the 2026-10 snapshot, choosing 2019 shows 2017 for Public Assistance.
Two layers can describe different years. The table, the scatter plot and the correlation use each layer's own data year.
In the Analysis tab the year chip for a survey series names the whole five-year window, for example 2020–2024, while the year bar counts it by its last year (2024).
The year bar in a shared link stores your choice. Without it the link opens at 'Latest'.

name: Trend line in the inspector and the Trend chart
plain: The small line beside each value in the workbench's Inspector, and the Trend view of the workbench, show how a layer's value moved across the years. A caption under each small line says how many years it covers. The Housing page profile has similar lines.
definition: The Trend column of the workbench's Inspector view shows the layer's calculated values (with the same rescaling, inflation and base-year settings) for each data year from 2010 on, as one small line per layer for the place you selected. The column header reads 'Trend' with 'years shown; dot = chosen year' under it. Under each line a caption gives the number of years from the first to the last (counting years with no data), then the span, in the form 'N yrs · 2014–25'. When some years have no value it adds the number of values, in the form 'N yrs, M values · 2010–25'. A dot marks the data year on the map. The line needs at least two values and is not drawn for one-time snapshots. The Housing page profile has lines of the same kind, drawn from every year the series has, with a caption of the number of years only ('N yrs'). The Trend view charts the places you click or add, with the layer's settings. It uses years from 2010 on, and from the first year for the three Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) datasets. It draws at most eight lines.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

method: Functions ecSpark and ecBenchTrend in site/js/economy.js and spark in site/js/housing.js. Each line in the Trend column (and on the Housing page profile) is scaled between that place's own lowest and highest value. The chart joins points across years with no value (spanGaps).
source_detail: Any dataset with more than one year in the Analysis tab; the Trend tab chart is drawn with Chart.js.
how_to_read: Use the line for direction and timing, then read the numbers in the table. The caption tells you whether the line covers a full run of years or has gaps. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) jobs read '12 yrs · 2014–25'. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) unemployment rate reads '16 yrs, 15 values · 2010–25' because it has no 2020 value. On the Housing page the resident population reads '16 yrs'.
caveats: Each small line is scaled to its own minimum and maximum, so the steepness of two lines cannot be compared between rows or between municipalities.

Where years have no value the chart draws a straight line across the gap, which suggests steady change. FEMA series have values only for years with a disaster declaration. The observatory's unemployment series has no 2020 value.
For survey series each year on the line is a five-year window, so '15 yrs' means 15 overlapping windows, not 15 separate years of responses.
The population series changes base in 2020 and survey windows overlap, which can bend or smooth a line (see the entries on both).
For a 'Change since the base year' layer the line starts after the base year.

The Trend view draws at most eight lines. Puerto Rico always comes first when it is chosen, then the municipalities in list order, so with more than seven municipalities chosen the last ones in the list are left out and Puerto Rico stays.
