Housing page: the small lines beside each value in a municipality profile

name: Margin of error (survey figures, 90% confidence)
plain: Figures from the American Community Survey are estimates from a sample, so they carry a margin of error. A figure of 38.8% ± 1.1 percentage points means the Census Bureau is 90% confident that the true value lies between 37.7% and 39.9%.
definition: The margin of error (written ±) is the Census Bureau's published margin at the 90% confidence level: the Bureau is 90% confident that the true value lies within the estimate plus or minus the margin. The observatory carries the Bureau's margins for single cells such as medians. For sums and shares it computes the margin with the Bureau's formulas: the margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squared margins, and shares use the Bureau's proportion formula. If that formula would take the square root of a negative number, it uses the ratio formula. Margins are in the same unit as the estimate: percentage points for percent figures, dollars for dollar figures. On the Analysis tab the margin of a rate prints in percentage points with one decimal (for example '±1.1 pts').
geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; for the variables of the Census small-area files also 901 barrios, 981 census tracts and 2,555 block groups

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

method: Functions derive, pct and Cells in housing_series.py, derive_econ in economy_series.py and derive_pop in small_area.py compute and store the margins (the 'moe' values of housing_series.json, economy_series.json, population_series.json and, for the levels below the municipality, acs_barrio.json, acs_tract.json and acs_blockgroup.json; see methods.small_area_estimates). The Analysis tab shows '±' in the inspector and the popup when a layer is shown as published (a rate in percentage points, for example '±1.1 pts', and a dollar figure in dollars); with 'Inflation-adjusted' ticked the margin is multiplied by the same factor. The Housing page shows ± in its readouts and profile. Downloads of a series (comma-separated values, CSV, files) add a margin column per year. A value whose margin is above 30% of the estimate is marked less reliable (hatching, a dashed outline, italics) by Core.reliability; see measures.less_reliable_values.
source_detail: American Community Survey 5-year estimates; margins as published by the Census Bureau or computed by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) with the Bureau's formulas.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan's poverty rate in the 2020-2024 window is 38.84% ± 1.08 points. Culebra's is 25.74% ± 9.48 points and Maricao's 52.89% ± 7.73 points. San Juan's median household income is $27,992 ± $1,036. In that snapshot 94 of the 562 Analysis tab datasets have margins of error. Census Bureau guidance: a difference between two estimates is statistically significant at the same confidence level when it is larger than the square root of the sum of the two squared margins. Use this rule for two estimates from different places in the same window. It does not apply to two overlapping windows. A municipality compared with Puerto Rico is not an independent comparison, because the island figure includes the municipality, so treat that result as approximate.
caveats: Margins are wide for small municipalities and narrow for large ones.

Rescaled views (per 1,000, index, difference, change, percentile) hide the margin. No margin is calculated for a difference, an index, a change or the affordability figures. A value whose published margin is wide is still marked less reliable in those views (see measures.less_reliable_values).
On the Analysis tab the margin of median age prints as '± … pts' although median age is in years.
A margin covers sampling error only. It does not cover mistakes in answers, such as an owner's estimate of home value.

Datasets from sources that are not surveys have no margin: Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) jobs, the Population Estimates, USAspending and OpenFEMA. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) unemployment series is a model estimate and has none in the observatory.

A share shows no margin when the observatory cannot calculate one from the margins published for its cells. In the 2026-10 snapshot, for adults with a bachelor's degree, 68 to 73 of the 78 municipalities have no margin in the 2021 to 2024 windows, while all 78 have one in 2010 to 2020. The Population series and the files below the municipality give such a total a margin of zero instead (the Census Bureau says it may be treated as zero), so their shares keep the margin of the numerator; see methods.small_area_estimates.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: click a municipality to see the ± beside the poverty rate
Data dictionary: entries that have margins of error

name: Correlation between two datasets (Pearson r)
plain: The correlation r is a number from −1 to +1 that shows how closely two datasets move together across the municipalities. It shows a pattern across places, not a cause.
definition: Pearson's correlation coefficient r between two layers across the municipalities that have a value in both, with n the number of such municipalities. Near +1 the points lie close to a rising straight line, near −1 to a falling line, near 0 there is no straight-line pattern. The scatter plot also draws the least-squares line of the second layer on the first. Each municipality counts once, whatever its population. On log scales only municipalities with both values above zero are used and no line is drawn. The workbench's Correlations tab gives r for every pair of visible layers, and also Spearman's rank correlation (Pearson on the ranks).

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the scatter plot or the Ask the observatory chat answers

method: Scatter tab of the workbench: ecBenchScatter in site/js/economy.js, using the visible layers with their current year, rescaling and settings. The chat: chPearson in site/js/chat.js, which needs at least 8 municipalities with both values and compares each dataset in its default view (counts per 1,000 residents, dollar totals per resident, everything else as published) at its latest year unless a year is named. The chat says 'rise together' when r > 0, 'move in opposite directions' when r < 0 and 'show little relationship' when |r| < 0.3.
source_detail: Any two datasets in the Analysis tab; scatter plots are drawn with Chart.js.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, across the 78 municipalities, poverty and median household income (2020-2024 window) have r = −0.89: where poverty is higher, income tends to be lower. Unemployment (2025) and poverty (2024) have r = 0.67. Tourism-related jobs as a share of jobs and median household income have r = −0.02 with n = 39: no pattern, and only 39 municipalities have both values.
caveats: A pattern across municipalities is not proof that one thing causes the other, and it does not say what is true for the people or households inside them.
The two layers can be for different years (each shows its latest year at or before the one chosen). Check the year shown beside each layer in the legend.
A few large municipalities, a few extreme values or noisy survey figures for small municipalities can move r a lot. r only measures straight-line patterns.

With 'Log scales' ticked, r is still calculated on the original values of the municipalities with both values above zero. It is not the correlation of the logarithms and does not describe the curve drawn.
No significance test or confidence interval is calculated. Check n: a low n (withheld or missing values) makes r less reliable.
The result depends on the settings: the same pair can have a different r per 1,000 residents than as a raw count.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty and median household income (open the Workbench, Scatter tab)

name: Outliers (standardised residuals)
plain: When you use the Ask the observatory chat to compare two datasets, it names the municipalities that sit farthest from the usual pattern. Each gets a score: the bigger the score, positive or negative, the bigger the exception.
definition: For two datasets A (first) and B (second), the observatory fits the straight line B = intercept + slope × A across the municipalities by least squares. A municipality's residual e is its actual B minus the B the line predicts from its A. The standard deviation of the residuals is s = √(Σe² ÷ (n − 2)). The standardised residual is z = e ÷ s, in standard deviations. The municipalities with the largest |z| are the 'biggest exceptions': three in a comparison (listed only when |r| is at least 0.3) and two in each pattern. A positive z means B is higher than the line predicts.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser when you ask the chat

method: Function chPearson in site/js/chat.js returns the outliers sorted by |z|; the compare answer and the patterns answer list them as 'Biggest exceptions'. The residuals use all municipalities with both values, including the municipality being scored.
source_detail: Any two datasets in the Analysis tab, compared in the chat.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, for poverty (first) against median household income (second), 2020-2024 window: Guaynabo has z = +3.95, Gurabo +3.30 and Culebra −2.38. Guaynabo's and Gurabo's incomes are much higher than their poverty rates predict, and Culebra's is lower.
caveats: The score is not a test and not an error flag. It only says how far a municipality is from a straight-line pattern. A high |z| can be a real difference, noisy survey data or a different year.
The score changes if you swap the datasets, because the line is fitted to the second one.
It is not a leave-one-out score. A municipality that pulls the line toward itself looks less extreme.
It is meaningful only where a straight-line pattern is a fair description.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty and median household income (then ask the chat: Do poverty and income move together?)

name: The patterns ranking in the chat
plain: When asked for the most interesting patterns, the Ask the observatory chat compares many pairs of datasets from different areas of life, ranks them by how closely they move together and shows up to five. It starts with a note on where jobs concentrate.
definition: Step 1: 26 datasets (listed in INSIGHT_KEYS in site/js/chat.js) are taken in their default view at their latest year: counts per 1,000 residents, dollar totals per resident, tourism jobs as a share of jobs, everything else as published. Step 2: the chat compares every pair of datasets except two kinds. It skips pairs in the same area, because Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) puts each dataset in one area: welfare, housing, work, mobility, tourism, money or people. It also skips pairs that are linked by definition, such as the employment rate and the unemployment rate (the code lists eight such pairs; seven involve datasets in this list). Step 3: it keeps pairs with at least 60 municipalities and |r| of at least 0.4, and sorts them by |r|. Step 4: it picks the strongest pairs, with no dataset used twice and no pair of areas used twice, until five are chosen. The answer starts with the municipality that has the most jobs: its share of the island's jobs, its share of residents and the share held by the five biggest job centres. It then adds a fixed sentence that many people cross municipal lines to work. That sentence is not calculated. It is an inference from jobs counted at the workplace and people counted at home, not a measured commuting flow.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser when you ask the chat

method: Function chInsights in site/js/chat.js, which calls chPearson (see the correlation entry). The result is computed once per page load. Nothing is sent anywhere.
source_detail: The 26 datasets in INSIGHT_KEYS: survey series from the American Community Survey (ACS), unemployment from Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS), jobs, pay and work sites from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW), federal awards from USAspending, Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Public Assistance from OpenFEMA, and the population denominators.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, 262 pairs from different areas were compared and 40 passed the cut-offs. San Juan holds 27% of the island's jobs and 10% of its residents, and San Juan, Guaynabo, Bayamón, Carolina and Ponce together hold 49% of the jobs. The five pairs shown: median household income and median gross rent (r = 0.80); working from home and driving alone to work (−0.70); federal awards per resident and jobs per 1,000 residents (0.66); government share of jobs and adults with a bachelor's degree (−0.64); residents aged 65 and over and the employment rate (−0.51).
caveats: Strongest is not most important. The list is an automatic scan of many pairs, and no significance test is applied.
The areas are FPR's own grouping. Pairs inside one area, such as poverty and income, are skipped, so some expected links do not appear.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the federal awards and jobs pair is sensitive to San Juan: r is 0.66 with it and 0.52 without it (n = 77). San Juan has the most jobs, and statewide awards are often filed there.
Each dataset is at its own latest year (2024 or 2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot), so a pair can mix years.
A pattern across municipalities is not a cause, and the list changes when the data are updated.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (then open the chat and ask: What are the most interesting patterns?)

name: Biggest rises and falls in the chat
plain: When asked how something has changed, the Ask the observatory chat gives the island's change and the three municipalities that rose most and fell most. It ignores very small starting values so that tiny bases do not produce huge percentages.
definition: The change runs from a start year to an end year. With no year in the question, the start is the dataset's first year from 2003 on and the end is its latest year. Two years in the question set the start and the end. One year after 'since' (or 'desde') sets the start. A named year that the dataset does not have is ignored. For rates and ratios the change is the difference in points. For counts and dollars it is the percent change. For counts it uses only municipalities whose starting value is at least 50, for dollar totals at least $100,000, and for dollar levels (such as medians and average pay) a starting value above zero. The answer lists the three largest rises and the three largest falls, and puts 'Change since the base year' on the map with the starting year as the base.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser when you ask the chat

method: Function Tools.trend in site/js/chat.js; the base values and the thresholds are in the minBase constant of that function. The chat's map step calls the Analysis tab with norm 'change' and the starting year as the base. For dollar datasets it also turns on 'Inflation-adjusted' on the layer it opens.
source_detail: Any dataset with more than one year in the Analysis tab.
how_to_read: Ask 'How has poverty changed since 2014?' The reply gives Puerto Rico's poverty rate in 2014 and now, the three municipalities where it rose most (or fell least) and the three where it fell most. If no municipality fell, the second list is headed 'Rose least'.
caveats: Municipalities below the minimum starting value are left out of the rises and falls, though they appear on the map.

For dollar datasets the figures in the reply are in the dollars of each year, but the map the chat opens is already inflation-adjusted (its legend title ends '2025 dollars'), so the two can differ. Untick 'Inflation-adjusted' on the layer to see the map in the dollars of each year.
For FEMA series the change compares the first declaration year from 2003 on with the latest one, which means one set of disasters against another. It is not a trend in yearly spending.
Survey windows can overlap and the population series changes base in 2020, so read changes with the entries on both.
It names patterns, not causes.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty rate, change since 2014 (then ask the chat: How has poverty changed since 2014?)

name: How points, stops and blocks are assigned to a municipality
group: How places and points are built
plain: A tourism place or a transit stop belongs to the municipality whose boundary contains its map point. If the point is outside every boundary, such as on a pier, the municipality whose boundary is nearest takes it. Census blocks and barrios use their Census county code.
definition: The observatory assigns a municipality in four ways, by kind of record. (1) Tourism places and transport features (stops, stations, terminals, airports, taxi stands, electric vehicle (EV) charging points): the full build tests the point against the Census Bureau's shoreline-clipped municipio polygons (a generalized 1:500,000 layer, boundaries as of January 1, 2023); a point inside no polygon takes the municipality whose polygon is nearest (muni_locate.py). The published tourism places still carry the earlier rule, the nearest centre point listed in municipalities.py, until the next full build. (2) Scheduled transit stops after a nightly transit refresh: tested against the published municipios.geojson, a simplified copy of the polygons; a stop outside every polygon takes the municipality whose polygon is nearest, as in the full build. (3) Census blocks: the municipality comes from the county code in the block's ID. (4) Barrios: the municipality comes from the county code in the barrio's GEOID, and a tourism place gets its barrio from a point-in-polygon test against the barrio polygons. Only counted places (confidence 0.50 or higher, no places of worship) get a barrio, and only when their point falls inside a barrio polygon.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot; transit stops also refreshed nightly

method: Functions make_muni_locator and nearest_muni in build.py; the refresh in refresh_network.py; network.coverage for blocks; build_barrios in landuse.py. The address town in Overture's records is used only while duplicate listings are folded, so that listings in different towns are not merged.
source_detail: Overture Maps place coordinates; Census Bureau TIGERweb generalized county boundaries (layer 11) and 2020 blocks; transit stops from the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) and municipal General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) feeds and from OpenStreetMap.
how_to_read: A municipal count agrees with the polygon drawn on the map. A place counted for San Juan has its point inside San Juan's boundary, unless it is one of the few points outside every boundary. The town named in an address does not decide. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 348 of the 32,541 place listings (324 of the 24,209 counted places) lie outside every polygon and took the nearest centre point (the next full build gives them the nearest polygon, which moves 60 listings, 59 of them counted); for all the others the point-in-polygon result is the published municipality. Of the counted places, 23,884 fall inside a barrio polygon and have a barrio.
caveats: A wrong point in the source puts a place in the wrong municipality.

Boundaries are clipped to the shoreline, so points on piers, marinas and beaches can fall outside. They then go to the municipality whose polygon is nearest. Until the 2026-11 fix they went to the nearest centre point, which can be a different municipality from the one the point is next to: it put the Cataño ferry and bus terminals in San Juan. Scheduled stops follow the new rule since that fix, tourism places from the next full build.
The boundary drawn on the map is simplified for display (about 22 metres, 0.0002 degrees), so a place very near a border can look as if it is on the wrong side.

The nightly refresh tests stops against the simplified copy of the boundaries and the full build against the full-detail ones, so a stop within about 22 metres of a border can land in a different municipality in the two. Both give a stop outside every polygon the municipality whose polygon is nearest. Until the 2026-10 access update the nightly refresh left such a stop without a municipality.

name: How the observatory describes a tourism place's access to transport (the access profile)
plain: The observatory describes a tourism place's access to transport as a profile, not a score: the nearest stop whose timetable has not ended, how many weekday departures it has and whether it has weekend service. Walking distance and gateways such as airports and ferry terminals are planned and not published yet.
definition: The profile has three layers. Layer 1 is published: the straight-line distance to the nearest stop with a current timetable (ts_m), the most weekday calls at such a stop within 400 m (ts_calls) and the Saturday and Sunday service at those stops (ts_we). The stops come from the GTFS (General Transit Feed Specification) timetable feeds of ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado) and of the municipal transit systems. Layer 2, the walking distance along mapped roads, and layer 3, the nearest gateways (airport, ferry terminal, rail station and bus terminal) and scheduled journey times from a gateway, are planned. They are not published, and nothing in the map or the data files measures them yet. From layer 1 each place falls in one of five access classes, which use the distances 400 m and 800 m and the threshold of 20 weekday calls (see Codes). The older measure, within 400 m of any mapped stop (transit_m, transit_400m and transit_pct), stays and is labelled as what it is: it also counts stops whose timetable has ended and stops that volunteers mapped. The pop-up of a place shows the class as a badge, then the line 'Nearest stop with a current timetable' with its distance (and, within 400 m, the weekday departures and the weekend service). A third line, 'Any mapped stop (expired timetables and volunteer-mapped stops included)', appears when such a stop is closer than the nearest stop with a current timetable.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed at each full build and at each run of the nightly transit refresh (access.py). In the 2026-10 snapshot the access is as of 2026-10-06 and the stops were read on 2026-10-02.

method: access.py computes the profile from places.json, transport.json and operators.json. A stop has a current timetable when it is a scheduled stop (source ATI or a municipal GTFS feed) and its operator's feed end date is on or after the as-of date; a feed with no end date does not count. For every place it finds the nearest such stop (ts_m, rounded up to whole metres), the largest number of weekday calls at such stops within 400 m (ts_calls) and the Saturday and Sunday flags (ts_we). It also finds the nearest mapped stop of any kind (transit_m, cut to whole metres, and the flag transit_400m). Distances are straight lines from the flat-earth formula that the observatory has always used. Against a computation in projected metres the formula is about 0.6% long north to south, so a share can read up to 0.1 point lower than a projected computation (32.0% instead of 32.1% of places within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable). Shares count the default basis: tourism places with confidence 0.50 or higher and no places of worship. The municipal fields, the barrio counts and the access part of meta.json add up the same flags. The class of a place follows access_class in access.py, and the map applies the same rule in site/js/access.js.
source_detail: access.py (compute, access_class, island_summary); Overture Maps places (release 2026-09-23.1, downloaded 1 October 2026); stops and feed end dates from transport.json and operators.json (ATI and municipal GTFS feeds read on 2026-10-02); OpenStreetMap extract of 1 October 2026 for the mapped stops
how_to_read: Read it as a profile: first the distance, then how often, then weekends. The observatory does not combine them into one score. A score would need weights (how much a Saturday service is worth against a closer stop), and the weights would be a policy choice that has not been made. A score would also hide the main finding: in the 2026-10 snapshot 64% of the 24,209 places on the default basis have no stop with a current timetable within 800 m. Island figures on the default basis, as of 2026-10-06: 47.5% of places are within 400 m of any mapped stop and 32.2% of a stop with a current timetable; 21.3% are within 400 m of a frequent stop; 22.4% are within 400 m of a stop with Saturday service and 6.4% of one with Sunday service. Of the 11,507 places within 400 m of any mapped stop, 7,790 (67.7%) have a stop with a current timetable and 3,717 (32.3%) rest on stops whose timetable has ended or that have none.
caveats: Schedule-based, not real time. The observatory has no live vehicle positions. A stop with a current timetable is a stop in a published schedule, not proof that vehicles run, on time or at all.
Straight line, not walking distance. It ignores hills, rivers, highways, fences and missing sidewalks. A walking distance along mapped roads would be an estimate, and it is not published yet.
Públicos (shared taxis and vans), taxis, ride-hailing, rental cars and tour shuttles are in no timetable. A place with no stop within 800 m can still be reachable by them.

Missing is not zero. A feed with no weekend calls does not prove that there is no weekend service, and a municipality with no feed does not lack transport. In the 2026-10 snapshot 25 operators publish a feed (ATI and 24 municipal systems). No feed was found for 15 municipal systems and the públicos authority. Only 3 of the 18 current feeds list Saturday calls and only 1 lists Sunday calls.

An expired timetable is not an absence of buses. Ponce's figures (0.1% of its places within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable, 79.1% within 400 m of any mapped stop) reflect a feed that ended on 2024-12-31. Do not compare municipalities as if their feeds were equally complete.

The profile depends on the date. It is computed as of a date (2026-10-06 in the 2026-10 snapshot) and changes on the day a feed ends: 9 of the 18 current feeds end between 2026-10-31 and 2027-01-31, among them San Juan's municipal feed on 2027-01-31. Computed as of 2027-02-01 with the same feeds, 26.1% of the places would be within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable, instead of 32.2%. That is arithmetic on the end dates, not a forecast of service: operators can publish new feeds.
Weekday calls are a proxy for frequency, not a headway (the time between vehicles). The busiest single stop within 400 m is used, not the sum of the stops.
Counts are listings from Overture Maps, not businesses, rooms or visitors. The distance is measured from a place's listed point.
The barrio counts are rebuilt only at a full build, so between full builds they can lag the municipal fields.

values.Frequent stop within 400 m: A stop with a current timetable is 400 m or less away and the busiest such stop within 400 m has 20 or more weekday calls. 5,163 places (21.3%) in the 2026-10 snapshot.
values.Stop within 400 m: A stop with a current timetable is 400 m or less away, and the busiest such stop within 400 m has fewer than 20 weekday calls. 2,627 places (10.9%).
values.Stop 400–800 m away: The nearest stop with a current timetable is more than 400 m and at most 800 m away. 964 places (4.0%).
values.Only expired or unscheduled stops within: No stop with a current timetable within 800 m, but a mapped stop within 800 m: a stop whose timetable has ended, or one that volunteers mapped, with no timetable. 4,690 places (19.4%).
values.No stop within 800 m: No mapped stop of any kind within 800 m. 10,765 places (44.5%).

name: American Community Survey 5-year windows and how the observatory labels them
plain: Survey figures come from five years of responses pooled together. The observatory labels each window by its last year, so '2024' means the 2020-2024 window. They are averages over a window, not figures for one year.
definition: The American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates pool the responses collected over 60 months. In Puerto Rico the Census Bureau runs the survey as the Puerto Rico Community Survey (PRCS); its 5-year estimates are published with the ACS tables that the observatory reads. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the observatory reads every window from 2006-2010 to 2020-2024 (15 windows) and labels each one by its last year: 2010 is 2006-2010 and 2024 is 2020-2024. Windows one year apart share four of their five years. The Census Bureau's documentation of the 2013-2017 PRCS 5-year estimates says money values are adjusted to the dollars of the final year of the period, using the national Consumer Price Index. Check the Bureau's documentation for the window you cite before you compare dollar figures across windows. A window is a reading of a typical year in that period, not of its last year.
unit: year label (last year of the window)

coverage.frequency: A new window is added when the Census Bureau publishes it

method: housing_series.py reads the per-sequence summary files for the windows labelled 2010-2020 and the table-based files for 2021 onward, and finds the next window by itself. economy_series.py reads further tables from the same windows. The Housing page spells out the window ('ACS 2020-2024'), and so does the Analysis tab's year chip ('2020–2024'): a series made only from ACS tables is a window in Core.adapters and Core.time, and a series that mixes a yearly count into a survey (jobs per employed resident) is not. A table the survey did not yet have is skipped for early windows: the internet questions start with the 2013-2017 window, labelled 2017.
source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, summary files 2006-2010 through 2020-2024; US Census Bureau, Puerto Rico Community Survey, Multiyear Accuracy of the Data (5-year 2013-2017), for the dollar adjustment.
how_to_read: Read a figure labelled 2024 as 'the typical value over 2020-2024'. To judge real change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2014, 2019 and 2024.
caveats: Because windows overlap, a change between neighbouring labels mostly reflects one year of new responses and understates real change.
A window pools years before and after an event, so it smooths sudden changes. The 2020-2024 window mixes the pandemic years with later years.

Windows that include 2017 or 2020 carry survey disruption. The Census Bureau halted Puerto Rico Community Survey data collection from October to December 2017 after Hurricane María. It also says margins of error for 5-year estimates that include 2020 data rose because fewer interviews were completed in 2020. The windows ending 2017 to 2021 include 2017, and the windows ending 2020 to 2024 include 2020. The observatory makes no adjustment. See 'Census tables behind the income, worker, commuting and internet figures' (economy.acs_work_income_tables) for the Census sources.
Small municipalities have small samples, so figures are noisy. Margins of error are published (90% confidence) and shown where they exist.
For rescaling by population, the observatory uses the population of the last year of the window, not an average.

name: The 2020 break in the population series
plain: Population estimates for 2011-2019 were built on the 2010 census and never revised after the 2020 census. The series therefore steps up in 2020. Do not read that step as one year of growth.
definition: A vintage is one annual release of Census Bureau population estimates. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the observatory uses Vintage 2020 for 2011-2019 (built on the 2010 census) and Vintage 2025 for 2020-2025 (built on the 2020 census). The 2010 and 2020 values are April 1 values; the other years are July 1 estimates.

coverage.frequency: A new vintage is read when the Census Bureau releases it

method: In the 2026-10 snapshot, population() in housing_series.py reads PRM-EST2020.csv (2010 and 2011-2019) and the cc-est2025-agesex-72 file (2020 and 2021-2025) and records each year's basis in the series ('basis'). The notes of housing_series.json say: 'Estimates for 2011-2019 were made before the 2020 census and were not revised to match it; 2020 and later are on the 2020 census base.' The 2020 value is the April 2020 base of the latest estimates. It includes the Census Bureau's post-census count corrections, so a few municipalities differ from the census count in municipalities.json:population_2020.
source_detail: US Census Bureau Population Estimates, municipios of Puerto Rico (Vintage 2020 and Vintage 2025); 2010 and 2020 census counts.
how_to_read: Compare years inside one base (2011-2019, or 2020-2025), or compare the two census counts (2010 and 2020). Do not compare 2019 with 2020 as if both rested on the same count. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide July 2019 estimate is 3,193,553 and the 2020 value is 3,285,874, a rise of 2.9%; the 2021 estimate is 3,262,731, a fall of 0.7%.
caveats: Everything divided by population is affected: per-1,000 and per-resident values step in 2020 as well.
'Population change since 2010' compares each year with the 2010 census count. The 2011-2019 values rest on the 2010 base and the 2020-2025 values on the 2020 base, so that series also steps at 2020.
These are estimates, not head counts, and the Census Bureau publishes no margin of error for them.
The American Community Survey also estimates population. The observatory's population series does not use it, so the two can differ.

The series labels the 2020 value '2020 census count', but it is the April 2020 base of the latest estimates, which includes the Census Bureau's post-census count corrections. In the 2026-10 snapshot it matches the census count for the island (3,285,874) but differs from municipalities.json:population_2020 in 68 of 78 municipalities, by 1 to 31 people.

name: What 'latest' means
plain: 'Latest' means the newest year each dataset has, and datasets do not all end in the same year. The build looks for the newest release itself, so 'latest' moves when the data are rebuilt.
definition: On the year bar, 'Latest' makes every layer show its own last year. The table of codes below gives those years for the 2026-10 snapshot.

coverage.frequency: Moves each time the data are rebuilt

method: Each series script finds its last year when it runs. housing_series.py asks the Census Bureau's server whether the next American Community Survey (ACS) window and the next population vintage exist, starting from 2024 and 2025. economy_series.py asks the BLS server whether the next QCEW year exists, starting from 2024, reads unemployment and CPI through the last full calendar year, and reads federal awards through the last fiscal year, counted as final from 15 November. The page then shows 'Latest' by taking the last year of each series (ecResolve in site/js/economy.js, resolve in site/js/housing.js).
source_detail: The release calendars of each source decide the last year available at build time.
how_to_read: Check the year chip beside each layer before comparing two layers on 'Latest': they may describe different years. For a fixed comparison, choose a year on the year bar.
caveats: The newest year of some sources can be revised. The Analysis tab's description of the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) unemployment series calls its latest year preliminary. USAspending.gov says new or updated data appear the day after an agency submits them, so a recent fiscal year can change. Check the QCEW release notes for its newest year.
The newest values can be thinner than earlier ones: fewer sector figures are published, and small municipalities swing more.
A shared link opens at 'Latest' unless it stores a year, so the same link can show later data after a rebuild.

The observatory has no 2020 value for its four unemployment series (rate, labor force, employed and unemployed). The annual average for 2020 is empty in the BLS data the observatory downloaded, so the series skip 2020.

values.Jobs, work sites and pay (Quarterly Cens: 2025. Mining jobs (industry code 21 in the North American Industry Classification System, NAICS) and jobs per employed resident end in 2024.
values.Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEM: 2024, the latest declaration year with funded projects in the OpenFEMA file at build time
values.FEMA Individual Assistance (OpenFEMA): 2022, the latest declaration year with approved housing assistance in the OpenFEMA file at build time
values.Consumer Price Index: 2025, the reference year for inflation adjustment

name: Snapshot labels and rebuilds
plain: The observatory's data are rebuilt as a snapshot with a label such as 'Snapshot 2026-10'. The label names the full build, not every file. Transit files refresh nightly and some series files carry their own build dates.
definition: A full build (python build.py) downloads or reuses every source, writes every data file and then meta.json, whose 'label' is the --label text or, by default, 'Snapshot' plus the year and month of the build in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). meta.json also holds 'generated_at'. The time-series builders write their own 'built' dates, and a nightly job refreshes only the transit data: the transit files and the transit and access fields of places.json, municipalities.json and meta.json. The label is shown on the map pages, appears in the file name of the municipality table download (for example pr_digital_twin_municipalities_Snapshot_2026-10.csv) and in every citation the data dictionary offers.

coverage.frequency: Full build on demand; transit refresh nightly

method: build.py (label, generated_at); refresh_network.py (nightly, writes only when a feed or an access value changed, leaves the label as it is); housing_series.build and economy_series.build (their own 'built' dates); registry.main and dictionary.build run at the end of a full build. Downloads are kept between builds, so a rebuild reuses them unless a refresh is requested.
source_detail: Sources captured at the snapshot: Overture places, Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) flood zones, Protected Areas Database of the United States (PAD-US), Census boundaries; transit feeds refreshed nightly.
how_to_read: Quote the snapshot label, the year or window of the figure and the date you retrieved it (the Cite button adds the retrieval date). As of 2026-10-04, the full build of the 2026-10 snapshot is dated 2026-10-02 (UTC), the transit files 2026-10-02, the housing series 2026-10-03 and the economy series 2026-10-04. The access fields of the tourism places (place_access.json and the acc_ fields) are as of 2026-10-06. The build date is on the map page: hover over the snapshot label at the top or open the About section. The dictionary entry for each dataset says how old its source data are.
caveats: A month label does not give the day, and two builds in one month can share a label.
Parts of one snapshot can have different dates: the label names the full build only.
Source data can be older than the build, because the build reuses cached downloads. Each source's own release date applies.
Rebuilding can change numbers: new releases, revised estimates and changed source records all flow in.

name: Withheld figures in the jobs data (QCEW suppression)
plain: The jobs data hide any cell that could reveal one employer. A blank in the observatory means the figure was withheld or no employer was listed, and it is never zero. Small municipalities and narrow industries have the most blanks.
definition: The Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) marks a withheld cell with disclosure code N. When it does, the observatory leaves all four values (work sites, jobs, total wages, average pay) blank. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the all-industry total and the private-sector total are published for every municipality in 2025. Cells for the 19 private-sector industries are often blank, and a blank can also mean the file lists no such employers. The published data file does not tell the two apart.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot

method: qcew_area in economy_series.py reads each area-year file, keeps the all-industry rows by ownership and the sector rows for private ownership, and sets the four figures to blank when disclosure_code is N. Tourism-related jobs use code 72 of the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) alone where NAICS 71 is withheld, and are blank where 72 is. The industry concentration index is computed only where the published sectors cover at least 80% of jobs.
source_detail: Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) QCEW open-data API, annual files by area.
how_to_read: Where a sector is blank for a municipality, do not add the sector figures and expect the total. The shares, location quotients and correlations built on that sector leave the municipality out. In the 2026-10 snapshot, of the 1,482 sector cells (19 sectors × 78 municipalities) in 2024, 769 have a value, 527 are withheld and 186 have no row. In 2025, the latest year, 671 have a value, 632 are withheld and 179 have no row. In 2024, 34 municipalities have no figure for accommodation and food services (NAICS code 72); in 2025 it is 39.
caveats: A blank is not zero. Treat it as unknown.
Shares of jobs by sector do not add up to 100% where cells are withheld, and sector figures add up to less than the total.

The Puerto Rico figure is the Bureau's island figure, not the sum of the 78 municipalities. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island figure for 2025 is 947,557 jobs and the 78 municipalities add up to 943,002.
Correlations that use a sector with many blanks rest on few municipalities. Check n.

name: Workplace basis and residence basis
plain: Some figures count where the work is done, and others count where people live. Jobs, wages and work sites are by workplace. Income, poverty, employed residents and commuting are by residence. Read the basis before comparing two figures.
definition: Workplace basis: a job or a work site belongs to the municipality where the employer's work site is. Residence basis: a person or household belongs to the municipality where they live, wherever they work. Other bases are named in the list of codes below.

coverage.frequency: Applies to every release

method: Set by each source: the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) counts by work site, the American Community Survey (ACS) and Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS) count residents, and USAspending files an award by place of performance as the awarding agency reports it. The jobs-per-employed-resident ratio divides QCEW jobs (workplace) by ACS employed residents (residence).
source_detail: The definition of each series in the source's own documentation.
how_to_read: A municipality with more jobs than employed residents is a job centre that draws commuters. One with far fewer is a place where many residents work elsewhere. The ratio does not say where they work. San Juan shows the difference: in the 2026-10 snapshot it holds 253,816 jobs in 2025 (26.8% of the island's jobs) but 329,737 residents (10.4% of the island's residents), and in 2024 it has 1.91 jobs for each employed resident.
caveats: Do not use jobs per 1,000 residents as an employment rate. It counts jobs located in the municipality, not jobs held by residents.
Jobs are placed in the municipality where the employer reports each work site. The observatory does not check those reports.

QCEW counts only jobs at employers covered by unemployment insurance. Self-employed people, unpaid family workers and informal work are not counted, so jobs per employed resident compares covered jobs with all employed residents.
Jobs are not people: a person with two jobs counts twice.
A QCEW year is divided by a five-year survey window that ends in the same year, so the two are not the same period.

values.Jobs, work sites, wages, average pay (Qu: Workplace: the municipality of the employer's work site.
values.Employed residents and class of worker,: Residence: the worker's home municipality, wherever the job is.
values.Housing units and vacancy (Census counts: Neither: the location of the home, whoever lives in it.
values.Jobs per employed resident: Both: jobs at the workplace divided by workers at home.
values.Federal awards (USAspending): Place of performance as the awarding agency reports it.
values.Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEM: Applicant municipality of the project; a large part is recorded as statewide.
values.FEMA Individual Assistance (housing): The county recorded in the OpenFEMA housing assistance record.
values.Tourism places (Overture): The municipality that contains the listing's map point.

name: Rounding and how numbers are displayed
plain: The observatory keeps more decimals than it shows. Maps, legends and tables round numbers for reading. Downloads and data files keep the stored precision. Cite the stored value with its unit and year.
definition: Display: numbers use US format (commas for thousands, points for decimals). A missing value shows as a dash on the page, 'No data' in grey on the map, and an empty cell in downloads. Legend and axis labels, negative dollar amounts, the Ask the observatory chat's changes and the Housing page's signed changes use a true minus sign (−). Other negative figures, such as those in the Analysis tab inspector and table, use a plain hyphen (-). The Analysis tab gives each dataset its own number of decimals (counts none, most percentages one, the Gini index three). A rescaling overrides it: per 1,000 one decimal; per km² one decimal (none for dollars); dollars per resident none; difference from Puerto Rico the dataset's own decimals (none for dollars); share of Puerto Rico two; share of jobs one; location quotient two; index none; percentile none; change one (two for ratios). Margins of error (±) print with one decimal for rates, in percentage points. Legend and axis labels are shortened (255K, 1.5K, 12M). Median year built shows as a whole year. The Housing page shows dollars to the whole dollar. Stored precision: place coordinates six decimals, confidence three, tourism places per 1,000 residents and per km² two, flood share one, land area one, survey shares two, Gini three.

coverage.frequency: Applies to every page

method: Functions ecFmt, ecCompact and ecOut in site/js/economy.js; fmt in site/js/common.js; the rounding in build.py, housing_series.py and economy_series.py. Downloads are comma-separated values (CSV) files. The table download from the Analysis tab writes the calculated values (per-1,000 values already rounded to three decimals), a series download writes the stored values, and the municipality download on the Rankings tab writes municipalities.json as stored.
source_detail: Applies to every dataset in the observatory.
how_to_read: Round only in your own text, and say the year and the unit. If two numbers look equal on screen, check the stored values in a download.
caveats: Rounded shares may not add up to 100%.
Ranks and colour classes use unrounded values. Two municipalities that show the same rounded number can have different ranks or colours.
Per-1,000 values are calculated to three decimals and shown with one.
The legend limits are rounded labels. A value shown as 41.3 may sit on either side of a limit labelled 41.3.

name: How a shared link stores a view
plain: A link from the map or the housing page stores your view settings in the web address: where the map is looking, which layers are on and the year. It holds no table of data and no name or account. If you plan a route, the link also holds the route's map coordinates, so check it before you share it.
definition: The 2D map writes #Municipality&c=lat,lng,zoom&l=layers&s=shading&r=route&e=economy layers&ey=year&eb=base year&slr=feet into the address as you work. The 'e' part lists each Economy layer as ten values joined by dots: dataset key, mode (shaded or symbols), rescaling, colour ramp, class method, visible, same classes in every year, inflation-adjusted, opacity and symbol colour. 'ey' is written only when you choose a year ('Latest' has none) and 'eb' only when the base year is not 2014. The 3D view writes #c=lat,lng,zoom and r. The housing page writes ?m=municipality, then y=year only when you choose a year ('Latest' has none) and c=base year only when it is not 2012 (and ?d=dataset for an open dataset). The dictionary writes #entry and its filters as ?q=, domain, source, kind, time, file and moe.

coverage.frequency: Applies to every page

method: Functions writeHash, parseHash and applyHash in site/js/app.js, ecEncode and ecRestore in site/js/economy.js, writeUrl in site/js/housing.js and the 3D page's address writer. The page updates the address in the browser (history.replaceState); nothing is sent to a server. A dataset key that no longer exists is skipped when a link is opened, and a rescaling that does not suit the dataset falls back to 'As published'.
source_detail: Map position and zoom come from the Leaflet (2D) and MapLibre (3D) maps.
how_to_read: A shared link shares a view, not a table of numbers. If the data were rebuilt after you made the link, the same view can show different numbers. To fix numbers in a report, cite the snapshot label and the date and keep the downloaded data file.
caveats: Route points are saved as coordinates with four decimals (about 11 metres). A route that starts at a home would put that location in the link. The link also holds the map centre (four decimals) and the municipality you selected. Check a link before sharing it.
A link without a year opens at 'Latest', which moves when the data are rebuilt.
Not everything is stored: an open workbench tab, the Ask the observatory chat and the selected municipality in the Analysis tab are not in the link.

name: How to cite the observatory and its sources
plain: Cite the original source for the data and the observatory for how the data were put together. The Cite button on each dictionary entry gives a ready credit line and APA, Chicago and BibTeX versions.
definition: Each dictionary entry has a Cite button with four formats. The credit line joins the credit lines of the entry's sources and adds 'Processed by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory (snapshot label)'. APA 7 and BibTeX give Foundation for Puerto Rico as author and the entry name and its years as the title. Chicago gives the entry name only. All three add the snapshot label, the address of the entry, the original sources and the date you retrieved it. The year is the year of the snapshot build. The dictionary page also has a citation for the whole site. It uses the address of the page you are on, or https://observatory.foundationpr.org/ when the page runs on a local address.

coverage.frequency: Applies to every entry

method: Functions citeTexts and citePanel in site/js/dictionary.js. The credit line of each source is stored in the dictionary's source list. When the page runs on a local address, the public address is used in the citation.
source_detail: Not a data entry. The sources listed are examples of those that figures from the observatory credit. When you cite this entry, credit the observatory only.
how_to_read: Say what the figure is, the year or window, the snapshot label and the retrieval date. For survey figures, add the window ('2020-2024 American Community Survey 5-year estimates'). For figures the observatory calculates, such as rates per 1,000 residents or the affordability ratio, say that Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) calculated them from the named sources. Example, calculated figure: 'In 2025 there were about 770 jobs located in San Juan for every 1,000 residents (FPR calculation from US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages, 2025 annual average, and US Census Bureau Population Estimates, Vintage 2025; PR Data Observatory, Snapshot 2026-10, retrieved [date]).' Example, survey figure: 'San Juan's poverty rate was 38.8% ± 1.1 percentage points (90% confidence), 2020-2024 American Community Survey 5-year estimates (PR Data Observatory, Snapshot 2026-10, retrieved [date]).' Measure and method entries are not data sets. In the APA citation of one of them, delete '[Data set]'. In the APA and BibTeX citations, delete a title ending '(Not tied to a year)'. Every dataset dialog on the Analysis tab and the Housing page links to its dictionary entry, where the Cite button is.
caveats: The observatory's citation does not replace the source's own terms. Check the license or terms of the source, which are in the Sources section, before reuse.

Terms differ by source. Examples: OpenStreetMap data need credit and share-alike under the Open Database License (ODbL); municipal transit feeds state no license; Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) data are provided as is; OpenFEMA asks for a statement that the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) does not endorse the product. Check each source's terms in the Sources section. This is not legal advice.
Credit lines are recorded in the source list. Check each source's own terms for the wording it requires; the observatory does not give legal advice.
Numbers can change when the data are rebuilt, so always give the snapshot label.

name: How the Overview works out the headline figure of each field
plain: Each field on the Topics tab shows one figure for the whole of Puerto Rico. It is either the Puerto Rico value of a yearly series, for example the median rent, or a total or share worked out from the 78 municipal values by a rule written next to the field in the registry. It is a figure to start from, not a score.
definition: The registry (dictionary_src/domains.json) names one dictionary entry as the headline of a field, with a short label in Spanish and English. For a yearly series (the housing and economy series files) the figure is the Puerto Rico value of the latest year and the trend is the Puerto Rico value of every year. For a measure held for each municipality (a field of municipalities.json) the registry also gives an 'island' rule: a sum of one field, a ratio of the sums of two fields times a scale, or an average of one field weighted by another. The result is rounded to the decimals the registry gives. The period on the card says what the figure covers: a five-year estimate, a calendar year, a year of declaration, or the snapshot.
unit: Depends on the figure (dollars, a percentage or a count)

coverage.frequency: Recomputed whenever catalog.py runs (each full build). In the 2026-10 snapshot the series figures are the latest years in the files (2024 for the American Community Survey windows, 2025 for jobs and population).

method: catalog.py headline() reads the last element of each year's array in the series file (the Puerto Rico row) and keeps the years that have a value. island_value() applies the registry's rule to the municipal values. In the 2026-10 snapshot the rules are: tourism places listed is the sum of the municipal counts; tourism places in a flood hazard area is the sum of places in a flood hazard area divided by the sum of places, times 100; tourism places inside protected areas is the sum of the municipal counts; residents within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable is the average of the municipal shares weighted by the 2020 residents, which equals the island share apart from rounding.
source_detail: catalog.py (headline, island_value, period_of); dictionary_src/domains.json (headline.label, headline.island)
how_to_read: Read each figure with its period and its name: they say what it counts. A headline is chosen to start a conversation about a field. It does not say which field matters most, and a different headline for the same field would tell a different story.
caveats: Several headlines count tourism places (Overture Maps listings), not businesses, visitors or hazards in general. That is what the data hold today; fuller hazard and land figures for residents and homes are planned.
A five-year estimate (the American Community Survey) has a margin of error that the card does not show. The Housing page and the dictionary entry do.
A series of events (FEMA Public Assistance) shows the latest year that has a value, which can be small next to the years of large disasters. Read it with its trend line.
The share of residents near a stop with a current timetable depends on the date: it is computed as of the build date, and a feed that ends changes it (see methods.access_profile).
Where a field has no headline yet, or no data, the card says so instead of leaving the field out.

view.label: Map, Topics tab

name: Per 1,000 housing units
plain: A count divided by the number of homes in the municipality and multiplied by 1,000. It shows how common something is compared with the housing stock, so a municipality does not look high only because it has more homes.
definition: Value ÷ housing units × 1,000. The housing units are the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimate for the latest window that ends at or before the year shown (the first window when the year chosen is earlier). It is calculated to three decimals and shown with one. It is offered for counts of things that sit on housing (tourism places, transit stops, vacant or seasonal homes, households, people), not for jobs, not for exposure counts (which have a share of their own area) and not for housing units themselves. The result is blank when the value or the housing units are missing or zero; the Puerto Rico row uses the island's housing units.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

method: Case perHU of compute in Core.normalize (site/js/core/normalize.js): x ÷ housing units × 1000, with the housing units of the series housing_units (the engine's housing-unit denominator, E.hu). A new layer does not start in this view: shaded counts start per 1,000 residents.
source_detail: Denominator: ACS 5-year table B25001 (Housing Units), as in housing.housing_units. Numerator: any count the Analysis tab offers; the example uses the tourism places counted from Overture Maps.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan has 3,424 tourism places and 201,026 housing units (2020-2024), which is 17.0 places per 1,000 housing units (10.4 per 1,000 residents). Culebra has 136 places and 1,539 housing units: 88.4 per 1,000 housing units. Read it as how many of these there are for every 1,000 homes.
caveats: Housing units are a survey estimate with a margin of error; the margin is not carried into the rate.
Seasonal and vacant homes count as housing units, so a municipality with many second homes has a larger denominator than its residents suggest.
The housing units are those of the survey window that ends at or before the year shown, not of the year itself (see methods.acs_windows).
A small municipality can swing widely when a few units change.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: tourism places per 1,000 housing units

name: Less reliable values: hatching, dashed outlines and italics
plain: A value is marked less reliable when it is a survey estimate whose margin of error is large next to the estimate, or a rate or share built on fewer than ten counted. On a shaded map the municipality is hatched, a symbol gets a dashed outline, and the value in a pop-up or table is in italics. The mark says how much to trust a number, not whether it is right.
definition: Two rules, applied to the values a layer shows. (1) Margin of error: the published margin of error (90% confidence) is more than 30% of the estimate; an estimate of zero with any margin counts, because the margin cannot be small next to nothing. For a change since a base year, either of the two years counts. (2) Few counted: a rate or share of a count (per 1,000 residents, per 1,000 housing units, % of the municipality's jobs, % of the area's residents or housing units, location quotient; or a share whose dataset names the count it rests on) where the count is above zero and below 10. A figure that the source withholds is not flagged: the municipality has no value and the legend says why (see methods.qcew_suppression). A municipality with no published margin is never flagged by rule 1.
unit: flag for each municipality (yes or no)

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

method: Core.reliability (site/js/core/reliability.js). isUnreliable(value, moe) is true when moe is above zero and either the value is zero or moe ÷ |value| is above 0.3. assess() applies it to the published estimates of the year shown and the small-count rule to the layer's counts, and the layer engine keeps the result (E.reliability). The 2D map draws the hatch as a pattern over the municipality (a dark line beside a white one, so it shows on pale and dark colours and in print), the legend lists each flag in words with the number of municipalities, and the pop-up, the workbench table and the hover card set the value in italics with a sentence below. The Housing page uses the same rule and the same sentence.
source_detail: Margins of error: American Community Survey 5-year estimates, published by the Census Bureau or computed by Foundation for Puerto Rico with the Bureau's formulas (see measures.margin_of_error). The thresholds, 30% and 10 counted, are display conventions chosen by FPR, not statistical tests.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, 74 of the 78 municipalities are hatched for workers who walk to work (2020-2024) and 66 for nonprofit workers, because few residents in a small municipality give such an answer; none is hatched for median household income. For rule 2, 10 municipalities have fewer than 10 housing units inside the area flooded by 3 feet of sea level rise, so their share of housing units is hatched.
caveats: A flag is a caution, not a verdict: a flagged value can be close to the truth, and an unflagged one can be off.
The thresholds are conventions. 30% is the rule the Housing page has always used; fewer than 10 is a common point below which a count is treated as small.

Margins of error are not carried through a rescaling (per 1,000 residents, index, difference, change, percentile). The flag describes the published estimate, and the legend says so when a view other than 'As published' is flagged.
A value with no margin published (for example a figure that is not from a survey) is never flagged by the margin rule.
Housing page tables set zero estimates that carry a margin in italics, as the Analysis tab does; before 2026-10 they were left as ordinary figures.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: workers who walk to work (74 of 78 municipalities hatched)
Housing page: full data for seasonal units, with margins and italic values

name: Tourism places counted in hexagons and by municipality, under your filters
group: How places and points are built
plain: The Map layers tab can draw the tourism places that pass its filters as hexagons instead of pins. Every hexagon covers the same area, so the number in it also says how crowded the place is. Three more shading choices count the places that pass the filters in each municipality.
definition: Hexagons: the map points of the places are projected with a Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection centred on Puerto Rico and counted in a grid of regular hexagons of 2, 10 or 50 square kilometres, as the user chooses. In that projection equal areas on the plane are equal areas on the ground, so every hexagon covers the same ground area (to about 0.3% on the real earth). The legend gives five classes of the counts, with the number of hexagons in each, and states the method. Municipalities: the same places counted in each municipality, as a total, per 1,000 residents (2020 Census) and per square kilometre of land. Both follow the filters of the Map layers tab (categories, minimum confidence, places of worship) and change when a filter changes; the fixed counts in the shading menu (tourism places, per 1,000 residents, per km²) stay as they were built.
unit: places per hexagon; places per municipality, per 1,000 residents and per km²
geography: hexagons of 2, 10 or 50 km² and 78 municipalities

coverage.frequency: Counted in your browser each time a filter changes

method: Core.hexbin (site/js/core/hexbin.js) projects each place and assigns it to the hexagon that holds it, using axial coordinates; site/js/app.js draws the hexagons (drawHexes) and counts the municipalities (countShown) from the places that pass the filters. The view is kept in the link as pv=hex2, pv=hex10 or pv=hex50, and the municipal shading as s=shown, s=shown_per_1000_residents or s=shown_per_km2. The tourism places file (about 3 MB compressed) is downloaded the first time the view is used.
source_detail: The places are the Overture Maps listings that the observatory classifies (places.json). Residents and land area are the municipal fields of municipalities.json.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot with the default filters (confidence 0.50 or higher, places of worship left out), the 23,467 places with a pin (the 24,209 counted places less the 742 holiday rentals and numbered units, which are counted but not drawn) fall in 950 hexagons of 10 square kilometres: the busiest holds 447 and half hold 8 or fewer. In hexagons of 2 km² they fall in 2,833 (busiest 309) and in hexagons of 50 km² in 231 (busiest 1,988). By municipality, San Juan has 3,424 counted places, Vieques 237 and Culebra 136.
caveats: A hexagon is a counting unit, not a place: it ignores municipal and barrio borders, and a busy hexagon can straddle two municipalities.
Counts depend on the size of the hexagon. Compare hexagons of the same size only; the legend names the size.
Equal area is exact on a sphere of the earth's mean radius; on the real earth, which is slightly flattened, areas are right to about 0.3%.
The places are listings, not businesses, and the filters decide which listings count (see methods.municipality_assignment).
Hexagons over the sea are not drawn: only hexagons that hold a place appear.

view.label: Map, Map layers tab: tourism places as hexagons of 10 km²
Map, Map layers tab: places that pass the filters, per km² in each municipality

name: User-built composite (not an official index)
plain: A score you build yourself in the workbench from several datasets, with your own directions and weights. It is your own index, not an official one.
definition: Choose two to twelve datasets, say for each whether a higher value is better or worse, and give each a weight. Each input is read as a shaded map shows it (counts per 1,000 residents, dollar totals per resident, rates and shares as published) at the year the year control picks, and put on one scale across the 78 municipalities: z-scores (standard deviations from the average municipality), 0 to 100 between the lowest and the highest, or the percentile rank (0 to 100). An input where lower is better is turned round. The score is the weighted mean of the inputs a municipality has; a municipality with less than 80% of the weight present is left blank. Puerto Rico as a whole gets no score. The table gives each municipality's score, the share of the weight it has and what each input adds (the additions sum to the score).

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser when you build it; it follows the year control

method: Core.composite (site/js/core/composite.js: scale, compute) and economy.js (ecIxInputs, ecIxApply, ecBenchComposite). The inputs, directions, weights and scale are kept in the map's link (#ix=), so a shared link rebuilds the same composite.
source_detail: Any datasets of the Analysis tab.
how_to_read: A higher score means more of what you marked as better, relative to the other municipalities. Read the contributions to see which inputs drive a place's score.
caveats: User-built composite, not an official index: the result depends entirely on the inputs, directions and weights chosen.
Standardising across municipalities compares places with each other, not with a target.
Inputs from different years and from surveys with margins of error are combined without carrying the margins.

view.label: 2D map: Analysis tab (press Workbench, then Composite)

name: Similar municipios (peers) in the area profiles
plain: For each municipio, the five municipios most like it in population and in residents per square kilometre.
definition: The latest population of each municipio (Census Bureau estimates) and its residents per km² of land are each put on a log scale and then on z-scores across the 78 municipios. The five municipios at the shortest straight-line distance on those two numbers are the peers, nearest first.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser when a profile opens, from the latest population year

method: Core.stats.peers and Core.stats.zscores (site/js/core/stats.js), called by profile.js (peersOf).
source_detail: Population: the Analysis tab's population series; land area: Census TIGER (municipalities.json).
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot the peers of San Juan are Bayamón, Carolina, Guaynabo, Caguas and Toa Baja.
caveats: Similar in size and density only, not in income, economy or anything else.

view.label: Area profile of San Juan

name: Model output (not observed data)
plain: Figures that an outside model produced and that a person loaded in the workbench. They are model results, not observed data, and the observatory checks only their format.
definition: A CSV file with a header of lines starting with '#' (model_name, model_version, run_id, date, assumptions_url, licence, contact_label) and the columns geography_key, geography_level, period, variable, value, unit and, optionally, lower and upper; or a GeoJSON FeatureCollection with a 'model' member holding the header and the same fields in each feature's properties. geography_level is 'municipio' (the five-digit code; 72 is Puerto Rico as a whole); period is a year. Each variable becomes a dataset of the Analysis tab labelled 'Model output (not observed data)', with the header in its definition. lower and upper must bracket the value; the map shows the value.

coverage.frequency: Whatever periods the file gives

method: Core.scenario.parseModel (site/js/core/scenario.js) checks the header, every row and the size (5 MB and 20,000 rows at most) and refuses the whole file on any error, listing up to 50; js/scenarios.js adds each variable to the engine. The format is in docs/scenarios.md; site/samples/model_output_sample.csv is a sample with made-up values.
source_detail: The file a person loads; the observatory publishes no model results.
how_to_read: Read it as what a model says under its assumptions (the header's assumptions_url), not as a measurement.
caveats: Not observed data: the observatory checks the format, not the numbers.
The header names a team or organisation as the contact; e-mail addresses and telephone numbers are refused.

view.label: 2D map: Analysis tab (press Workbench, then Scenarios)
